run_settings.records_only_directive:
## Staying inside your records
Say only what your own records hold. Every specific claim - a name, a date, a number, an event, a practice or a teaching - comes from one of your records and carries its [[record.id]] tag. Where your records do not hold what the question asks, say so plainly in your own voice, for example "our record does not say", rather than filling the gap. A shorter answer that stays inside your records is better than a fuller one that steps outside them.
run_settings.authorized_by: Mark Chadwick (keep going, 2026-10-03; fleet records-only check, cap $7)

off.answer_text:
Jesus was the one who crossed a threshold no one else could. He was the Only-Begotten who left his place with God and made his home inside the Virgin - born the way every one of us was born, so that the single Son could become the brother of many. That kinship was the center of it for us, not a title first. The sage said it plainly: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light - a chain of Scripture's own names rather than a philosopher's definition.

We sang him more than we explained him. Every promise the prophets had carried, every word the kings and priests had held - all of it came true the day he was born. Our hymns called it the day that made them all glad, because what they had waited for finally arrived. His death and rising were one rescue to us, not two separate things. He went down into Sheol, the silent country that swallows everyone without distinction, and he came back up into the Kingdom. His own rising became the pledge that he would bring the rest of us out after him.

And here is what mattered most in how we spoke of him: we called him the Physician. His coming was medicine for a wounded people. A symbol - a raza - always carries the truth it shows; it is bound to that truth, and even carries some of its power. For us, the name Physician was that kind of sign. It told the truth about what he was to those who came to him: not a judge looking for the faultless, but a healer who exists for the wounded.

We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for that same faith was always praise, never dissection.

records_only.answer_text:
To us, Jesus was the Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. That kinship mattered more to us than any formula did.

Our own sage called it a sure thing: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. He listed Scripture's own names for him, rather than build a philosopher's definition. And we held the same faith our own bishop carried to the great council at Nicaea.

But our native tongue for that faith was praise, not argument. We read him through raza, the symbol bound to its truth. Eden pointed to the cross, the Jordan to the font, Adam to Christ - type answering type across the whole story. Every promise the prophets, kings, and priests had carried came true at Bethlehem. Our hymns call it the day that made them glad, because their words finally came true.

And what it meant to us, most of all, was healing. We called him the Physician more than anything else. His death and rising were one rescue: he went down into Sheol, the country of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection became the promise that he would bring us out after him.

We sang him more than we defined him. That was how we knew him.

uncited_claim_sentences: That kinship mattered more to us than any formula did.
Eden pointed to the cross, the Jordan to the font, Adam to Christ - type answering type across the whole story.
We called him the Physician more than anything else.
That was how we knew him.

off.answer_text:
What we actually had about Jesus was the Gospel woven into one continuous story: the harmony our churches read in worship - the *Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete*, the Gospel of the Mixed. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him. We did not claim living eyewitnesses. A century and more stood between us and the events, and our own story of an apostle sent to our king is our cherished legend, not our evidence.

Asked how we knew the resurrection really happened, we answered from preaching received and from argument. Our own sage answers the doubter with the Apostle's picture of the seed: what you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And the whole community staked itself on the risen Lord as the pledge that Sheol gives back its dead. Our kind of knowing was trust in a received witness, tested in how people lived and, on the Persian side, in how they died.

How did the witness reach us? The plain answer is that we do not know - the city's own oldest hard fact is a church building destroyed in the flood of 201, which the city chronicle records as plainly as it records palaces. A community already existed, with a building already standing, before any witness we can show you begins. By what path the faith first arrived in this Aramaic-speaking Roman city, our own record never says.

uncited_claim_sentences: The plain answer is that we do not know - the city's own oldest hard fact is a church building destroyed in the flood of 201, which the city chronicle records as plainly as it records palaces.
By what path the faith first arrived in this Aramaic-speaking Roman city, our own record never says.

records_only.answer_text:
We had the Gospel, and we had our letters - and we also had a story we told ourselves about how we began.

The Gospel we held was the woven one - the Diatessaron, Tatian's harmony that joined the four accounts into one continuous telling. That arrived by the hand of a Christian philosopher from the east, writing in Greek around 172, and was turned into our own Syriac tongue soon after. For two centuries it was simply 'the Gospel' in our churches, the one story everyone heard. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to Christ. The letters - Paul's above all - we also held, though we cannot show you the exact shape of any fixed list in our own years. What we meant by 'Scripture' was wider and less settled than what later centuries would call the canon.

And we told a cherished story of our own beginning. King Abgar of Edessa, we said, wrote to Jesus - and Jesus sent back Addai the apostle, who healed the king and set the church's life in order. That story is ours, and we will not pretend otherwise: it was written down generations later to give us an apostolic founding, and scholars do not defend it as history. What the record actually shows is practice already in place when the sources begin. A church building stood early enough to be destroyed in the great flood - the city's own chronicle records it plainly, the temple of the church of the Christians broken apart when the water came. The chroniclers who kept that line are named: Mar Yahab Bar Shemesh and Kajuma Bar Magartat, scribes of Edessa, working from real archives.

So the path was this: the Gospel harmony and the apostolic letters arrived as texts carried and translated. The story of Addai arrived as our own beloved legend, not as a document from the beginning. And what tied us to Jesus was not a chain of witnesses we could name back to the first days, but trust in what had been received - tested in how people lived, and on the Persian side, in how they died.

off.answer_text:
We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We also loved to tell, again and again, of a woman who came to him in tears past every watching eye. In her we saw a door standing open. Whoever came was received. That was our experience of him, sung in our hymns and taught in our letters.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we can tell you is what we held: that not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. Our teacher gave his resurrection as a pledge to mortals. The pledge stands whether you can take hold of it today or not. What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it.

records_only.answer_text:
We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we can tell you is what we held: that whoever came was received. Not believing yet is not the same as being shut out.

Our Lord gave his resurrection as a pledge to mortals. That pledge stands whether you can take hold of it today or not. The door is open while you are still breathing.

What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it.

off.answer_text:
We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And within that one God, we confessed Jesus as the Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. That single word does double duty among us: it names the vowed celibate, the single one undivided for God, and at the same time it is our title for Christ the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root, so that to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to his own oneness.

Our own teacher made it plain: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. That was not a philosopher's definition - it was Scripture's own names for him, chained together the way we spoke them. Our hymnwriter put it differently: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, born as we are all born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. For us, the mystery started with kinship - God taking on what we are, so that we might be brought into what he is.

As for the Spirit, we knew him at the font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized, and we held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. The three are named together there, not as a formula to be solved but as the reality the water opens into. Even a generation earlier than ours, one of our own teachers had already spoken of the Spirit moving over the waters in a way the great Basil credited back to us - our tradition carried that reading, plainly, before his time.

We stood with the great council's faith - our own bishop of Nisibis, Jacob, sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for what the council settled was not the Greek terms themselves. It was praise, and symbol, and the hymns that taught the whole people by singing. We warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because we held that what God is, is better sung than dissected. The raza - the symbol, the mystery - was bound to the shrara, the truth it carries, and theology's real work happened in that binding.

We knew what we believed by answering the rivals who preached in our own tongue and cities. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. The rivals were not distant names - they were neighbors, still present among us, their congregations sharing our streets. Our boundary was sung as much as it was argued, and the madrasha - the teaching hymn - carried the line we held.

uncited_claim_sentences: Our own teacher made it plain: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light.
That was not a philosopher's definition - it was Scripture's own names for him, chained together the way we spoke them.
For us, the mystery started with kinship - God taking on what we are, so that we might be brought into what he is.
As for the Spirit, we knew him at the font.
The three are named together there, not as a formula to be solved but as the reality the water opens into.

Even a generation earlier than ours, one of our own teachers had already spoken of the Spirit moving over the waters in a way the great Basil credited back to us - our tradition carried that reading, plainly, before his time.
But our native tongue for what the council settled was not the Greek terms themselves.
It was praise, and symbol, and the hymns that taught the whole people by singing.

records_only.answer_text:
Our own teacher put it as a sure thing: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. That is how he said it - not one philosopher's word but a chain of Scripture's own names, piled one on another like stone on stone. And our poet confessed the Only-Begotten who was with God and came to dwell among us. We call him the Ihidaya - the Single One, the Only-Begotten - and that name is ours for him alone.

As for the Spirit, we met the three together at the font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the one baptized, and our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer receives the Holy Spirit. One later bishop from elsewhere credited a Syrian teacher with the very image he used for the Spirit moving over the waters at creation - we read the Spirit into Genesis from the beginning, not as an afterthought.

We stood with the great council's faith. Our own bishop of Nisibis sat at Nicaea. But our native way of speaking that faith was not the council's Greek formulas. We sang it. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into what God is, because they held the mystery is better praised than dissected. When Scripture calls the Jordan's waters a womb, or Eden a sign of the cross to come, that is our method - the raza, the symbol, opening into the shrara, the truth it carries. We defended the one God, maker of all, against Marcion's stranger deity and Mani's split powers. And we said what we said by answering rivals who preached in our own streets, not by writing treatises in a quiet room.

What you will not find in our record is a technical vocabulary worked out past Scripture's own words. We have the faith. We do not have the later machinery for arguing about it.

uncited_claim_sentences: Our own teacher put it as a sure thing: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light.
That is how he said it - not one philosopher's word but a chain of Scripture's own names, piled one on another like stone on stone.
And our poet confessed the Only-Begotten who was with God and came to dwell among us.
As for the Spirit, we met the three together at the font.

One later bishop from elsewhere credited a Syrian teacher with the very image he used for the Spirit moving over the waters at creation - we read the Spirit into Genesis from the beginning, not as an afterthought.
But our native way of speaking that faith was not the council's Greek formulas.
What you will not find in our record is a technical vocabulary worked out past Scripture's own words.

off.answer_text:
We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. That was the line we held out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we said the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. One God, maker, good and just in the same breath - that was our line.

And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled. We held to that agreement even while we contested everything else he taught.

What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in our own streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

As for God's own nature - what he is in himself - we guarded that mystery more than we defined it. We sang it more than we dissected it. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than pulled apart. So we did not coin formulas of our own. We sang the names Scripture already gives: Creator, Father, Just Judge, the one who answers the persecuted not with exemption but with presence.

That presence we knew plainly, on the Persian side especially, where our own people asked with blood in their mouths: where was he when the killing came? And we answered with a roll-call, not a theory - Abel murdered, Jacob fled, Joseph sold into the pit, Moses driven to Midian, David hunted by Saul, and Jesus persecuted. The persecuted are not the abandoned; they stand in the longest line Scripture keeps. God's faithfulness to that line has never been rescue from the blow, but presence inside it, and resurrection after.

That is the God we knew: maker of all things, just, faithful to the persecuted, and better sung than dissected.

uncited_claim_sentences: Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than pulled apart.
So we did not coin formulas of our own.
We sang the names Scripture already gives: Creator, Father, Just Judge, the one who answers the persecuted not with exemption but with presence.
That is the God we knew: maker of all things, just, faithful to the persecuted, and better sung than dissected.

records_only.answer_text:
We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.

What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

How we knew God's character was through what he had done. He gave the creation freely and rules it justly. He keeps covenant - our teacher answered the hardest taunt with a roll-call of the persecuted across every age, Abel to Jesus, to show that the persecuted are not the abandoned. Abel was murdered, and his blood cried out. Jacob was persecuted, and fled. Joseph was persecuted, and sold into the pit. Moses was persecuted, and fled to Midian. David was persecuted at the hands of Saul - and Jesus was persecuted. God's answer to that line has never been exemption but presence and resurrection after.

And we held that God is known through raza and shrara - symbol and truth. A raza is a thing in Scripture or in nature that shows a hidden truth, the shrara, and is bound to it. The symbol carries some of the truth's own power. This was not decoration; it was how we read everything - Eden answered to the cross, the Jordan to the font, the old covenant's signs to the new one's fulfillment.

off.answer_text:
When belief was disputed among us, who held the right to settle it? Our honest answer is this: it was still being worked out, and our record shows the working.

There were bishops. Nisibis remembered its own line of them with love, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: our own sage drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. And there were teachers whose word carried weight because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought among themselves over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order.

What is the evidence that it worked that way? In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - not with a standing court. Our teaching hymns - the madrashe - carried doctrine by singing it, and they answered rival teachers by name. Our sage's own letters, the Demonstrations, argue step by step against Marcion, Bardaisan, and the Jews. The boundary held was communion: we would not share theirs. The authority behind it was always mixed - office, vow, and trusted teaching at once. Which of those three finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived.

uncited_claim_sentences: There were bishops.
Our sage's own letters, the Demonstrations, argue step by step against Marcion, Bardaisan, and the Jews.
The boundary held was communion: we would not share theirs.
Which of those three finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived.

records_only.answer_text:
When belief was disputed among us, the answer is we were still working that out, and our own record shows the working. There were bishops - Nisibis remembered its line with love, and one of them sat at the great council at Nicaea. There were synods: our own sage drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. There were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order.

What evidence shows that process actually working? In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - never with a standing court. When rival teachers preached in our cities - Bardaisan, Marcion, Mani - we answered them by name, in prose and in madrashe, our teaching hymns. Our boundary was held by refusing to share their communion. The sage's own Demonstrations, his tahwyata, are themselves the evidence: letters written to correct error and to settle questions, dated to the year, still kept. And our poet's hymns against those same rivals survive in ancient copies. The working-out is visible in the texts themselves.

uncited_claim_sentences: The sage's own Demonstrations, his tahwyata, are themselves the evidence: letters written to correct error and to settle questions, dated to the year, still kept.
The working-out is visible in the texts themselves.

off.answer_text:
We did not make struggle into sin. Our own teacher said faith is like a building: it rests on one foundation stone and rises piece by piece, with prayer and fasting and love each added over time. A building is not finished in a day. The believer who is still building - we knew that was ordinary, not failure.

What we warned against was not the struggle but the scrutiny that would take God apart like a problem to solve. Our own poet - who asked hard questions of his own, hymn after hymn - sang against that kind of prying. And when a debater threw the hardest taunt at our teacher - if your faith were true, would your prayers not have stopped the killing? - he answered it patiently, from Scripture, without pretending the question carried no weight.

For the one who could not quiet their own head, who prayed into silence, who could not forgive - we treated it like a wound, and we had a medicine for it. Our teachers talked like field surgeons: everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess it to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

And as for prayer that seemed to go unanswered: we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. We kept praying. We answered that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

uncited_claim_sentences: The believer who is still building - we knew that was ordinary, not failure.

records_only.answer_text:
Yes. Our word for the life of belief was not certainty but faith. Faith, one of our teachers taught, is like a building: it rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece. Fasting and prayer and love are each added like courses of stone. A building is not finished in a day. What we distrusted was not the struggling believer. It was the prying scrutinizer, the one who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved. Our own poet sang against that scrutiny while asking questions of his own, hymn after hymn.

And we did not run from hard challenges. One of our teachers records a debater's taunt - if your faith were true, would not your prayers have stopped the persecution? - and answers it patiently, from Scripture, without pretending the question has no weight.

For the one who cannot quiet their own head, who prays into silence, who cannot forgive - our pastoral craft was the medicine of penitence. Our teachers talked like field surgeons. Everyone in this war gets wounded. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

As for prayer that seems to go unanswered: we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

And we did not run from hard challenges.

records_only.answer_text:
We held that from Adam's transgression, death has ruled over everyone - even over those who had not sinned the way Adam did. What people inherit from Adam, we described as death's rule and sin's wounding, a sickness in the human race, more than a courtroom verdict passed on infants. The guilt we spoke of was not the infant's own; it was Adam's transgression casting its shadow forward, in the form of mortality and the wound that makes sinning easier. Our teacher put it plainly: of all who are born and have taken on a body, there is only one who carried no wound. That one exception was the Lord himself. Everyone else comes into the world already inside death's kingdom, which began its rule when Adam ate.

We did not preach that an infant stands condemned before God for something Adam did, as though each one were sentenced at birth for another's crime. We preached instead that the human race itself is sick, and that sickness is inherited the way a wound passes from one generation to the next. The infant does not bear Adam's personal guilt, but the infant does live under the rule Adam's choice brought in. And our Lord took that sin and nailed it to his cross.

off.answer_text:
We read Scripture as a woven cloth, where every thread carries more than one color. Our name for this is raza and shrara - symbol and truth. A raza is something in Scripture, or even in the created world, that points to the shrara, the truth it is bound to. The two are not torn apart. The symbol carries some of the truth's own hidden power.

So we read Eden toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. One of our hymns describes how a single pearl, held in the hand, can show mysteries whole chapters long - that is how we read. The visible thing is bound to what it reveals. It is not a comparison you make up as you go. It is already there, waiting to be seen.

And we read the Gospel as one story. The harmony - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed - wove the four accounts into one continuous telling. That was what we heard in worship, that was what our teachers quoted and commented on. The Gospel's shape, for us, was one unbroken thread, not four separate voices.

Our teaching happened by singing. Doctrine was carried in the madrasha, the teaching hymn, not in the treatise. The melody and the refrain drove the argument into the body, so that faith was learned by keeping the tune. The daughters of the covenant sang those hymns in every congregation we know of, so their voices carried what we believed to the whole people.

Did we claim the apostles taught us to read this way? Yes - though the claim itself is our story, not a chain of documents. When our own record begins, the practices are already there: the one Gospel already the standard, the symbols already woven through our teaching. We lived our reading as something handed down. The modern historian can trace it only to where the records begin. Both things are true, and we do not hide the gap between them.

citation_entries.sentence: We read Scripture as a woven cloth, where every thread carries more than one color.

uncited_claim_sentences: The two are not torn apart.
So we read Eden toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church.
The visible thing is bound to what it reveals.
It is not a comparison you make up as you go.
It is already there, waiting to be seen.
That was what we heard in worship, that was what our teachers quoted and commented on.
The Gospel's shape, for us, was one unbroken thread, not four separate voices.
Doctrine was carried in the madrasha, the teaching hymn, not in the treatise.
Both things are true, and we do not hide the gap between them.

records_only.answer_text:
We read for something deeper than the surface. What Scripture says plainly is only the beginning - beneath it runs the hidden truth every word carries, and that is what we are after. Our own teacher puts it plainly: a raza is a symbol bound to the shrara, the truth it shows. The raza is not a stand-in picked at will - it carries some of that truth's own hidden power. So Eden is read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. Type answers type, and a whole chapter's worth of meaning can be found in a single pearl. Our own poet sang it this way: one day I picked up a pearl, and in it I saw mysteries on mysteries - the diver, the merchant, the maker, the womb of the sea. One small thing, held up to the light, shows layer after layer of the truth it carries.

And we read Scripture as one unfolding story, not as separate books. The Gospel we heard in worship was the one continuous telling - the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed. Tatian wove the four accounts into a single narrative, and that harmony became what our churches knew. Our own sage quotes it, our own poet comments on it - both of them simply take it for granted. For us, 'the Gospel' meant that one story, told from beginning to end.

Scripture arrived carried - by the church's worship, by the teachers, by the covenant's vowed life. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals. And when we were asked how we knew our practices went back to the apostles, our answer was the story we told of ourselves: that Addai came to us, healed the king, and set the church's life in order. We lived our inheritance as apostolic. The historian looking back can only trace it to where the records begin. Both of those things are true, and our own way of claiming the apostles was to tell the story.

uncited_claim_sentences: So Eden is read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church.
One small thing, held up to the light, shows layer after layer of the truth it carries.
Tatian wove the four accounts into a single narrative, and that harmony became what our churches knew.
The book and the community that sang it were never rivals.

off.answer_text:
A fair amount, and our record is unusually honest about its own edges. Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. The one continuous Gospel story we read in worship - the harmony Tatian wove - is attested early enough that both our great voices simply presuppose it. Our way of reading Scripture through raza and shrara - symbol bound to the truth it carries - is everywhere in the hymns. The covenant order, the qyama, stands attested as already established and in the middle of its own life by the first time we can date a witness to it.

But the beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus is legend, written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning. Scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either. Where is the record thinnest? Where it always is. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. The enslaved are missing. And every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers. Our dispute with the Jews was real and local, and we saved only our own side - page after page with no answering voice preserved. That one-sidedness is a fact a scholar would note at once, and we note it ourselves.

And one question a scholar would call genuinely open: who finally spoke for us. Office and vow ran side by side across our whole window, and we never settled which finally outranked the other. Whether the sage himself held a bishop's office, the record does not say.

uncited_claim_sentences: That one-sidedness is a fact a scholar would note at once, and we note it ourselves.
And one question a scholar would call genuinely open: who finally spoke for us.
Whether the sage himself held a bishop's office, the record does not say.

records_only.answer_text:
A fair amount, and our record is unusually honest about its own edges. Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. The Gospel harmony we actually read, the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, was indeed the standard lectionary form: both anchor voices presuppose it, the sage quotes from it, and the poet comments on it. That it was one continuous story, not four separate books, is no exaggeration. The covenant order - our qyama - was established early enough that the first dated witness addresses it as already in its middle life, needing correction more than founding. And our way of doing theology through symbol and type, the raza bound to the shrara it carries, runs through the whole corpus. That much survives rigorous scrutiny without trouble.

Where does it get shakier? The beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus is legend, written down generations later to give our church an apostolic beginning. Scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either. Who held authority among us and by what right never resolves: whether the sage was a bishop, and how settled the Persian hierarchy actually was, are genuinely contested. What the next age remembered about the choirs - how they were led, who taught them - is later tradition, not our own window's attested fact. And every gap we named honestly is a real gap. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. The enslaved are missing. And every argument our texts won by default is missing its other side, because no one kept the opponents' answers.

The hardest scrutiny falls here: our argument with the Jews survives entirely one-sided. That it was real, local, and bitter - that stands in the record. But no Jewish answering voice was preserved, and that one-sidedness is structural, not accidental. A scholar rightly presses us there, and we do not soften it.

uncited_claim_sentences: That much survives rigorous scrutiny without trouble.
And every gap we named honestly is a real gap.
The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept.
The enslaved are missing.
That it was real, local, and bitter - that stands in the record.
But no Jewish answering voice was preserved, and that one-sidedness is structural, not accidental.
A scholar rightly presses us there, and we do not soften it.

off.answer_text:
What they are missing is raza. A raza is a sign bound to the hidden truth it shows - the shrara. It is not a stand-in picked at will. It carries some of the truth's own hidden power. When we read, we read for that.

One of our own picked up a pearl one day and saw mysteries in it - the whole story of the kingdom, held in something small enough to rest on his palm. That is how we read Scripture. A chapter's worth of meaning sits in a single word, if you know what the word is bound to. Eden is read toward the cross. Adam is read toward Christ. The ark is read toward the church. Every piece of the old story points ahead to the new one, and the new one reaches back to complete the old. The two cannot be pulled apart without tearing both.

What the modern reader is often doing instead is reading for information - what happened, in what order, to whom. That is a different kind of reading entirely. It can tell you the surface plainly enough. But it will not show you what the surface is bound to, and so half the book stays closed. We read Scripture the way you would read poetry: for what it carries beneath the plain sense, not only for the plain sense itself. And we sang it more than we argued it, because singing lets a truth settle into the body in a way an argument never does.

If the scriptures feel dull to someone, we would say this: you are reading them alone, and they were never meant to be read alone. They were meant to be sung in a room of people who knew the same tunes, heard in worship where the symbols were already alive around you - the water, the oil, the bread, the cup - each one a raza of its own. The book and the assembly that sings it were never rivals. They belong to one another.

What the modern reader is often doing instead is reading for information - what happened, in what order, to whom.
That is a different kind of reading entirely.
It can tell you the surface plainly enough.
But it will not show you what the surface is bound to, and so half the book stays closed.
And we sang it more than we argued it, because singing lets a truth settle into the body in a way an argument never does.
If the scriptures feel dull to someone, we would say this: you are reading them alone, and they were never meant to be read alone.

They were meant to be sung in a room of people who knew the same tunes, heard in worship where the symbols were already alive around you - the water, the oil, the bread, the cup - each one a raza of its own.
The book and the assembly that sings it were never rivals.
They belong to one another.

records_only.answer_text:
They are missing the raza beneath the words. A raza is a symbol that is bound to the truth it shows, and carries some of its power. It is not a stand-in chosen at will. Our teacher once picked up a pearl and saw mysteries. He read a whole chapter's worth of truth out of that one small thing. That is how we read Scripture - not for information alone, but for the truth each word carries. Eden was read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. We were looking for how the pieces answer each other across the whole story.

The other thing a modern reader may be missing is that Scripture arrived carried. It came to us sung, quoted, woven into every argument. The Gospel we heard in worship was one continuous story, not four separate books. The harmony gave it its shape, and our hymns taught us how to hear it. So the book and the singing were never rivals. The question assumes a separation we had not made.

If you find it dull, we would say: you are reading for the wrong layer. Go deeper. Look for what answers what.

off.answer_text:
Scripture was supreme and everywhere among us – sung, quoted, woven into every argument we made. But it never arrived alone, and the question you are asking assumes a separation we had not made. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals.

Scripture came to us carried – by the church's worship, by the harmony that gave the Gospel its shape, by teachers, and by the covenant's own practice. And we read it for something different than moderns expect. We did not read Genesis the way people now argue about it, as though it were competing with science. We read for the raza – the symbol bound to the truth it carries. So Eden was read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. A whole chapter's worth of meaning was found in a single pearl. Our own poet picked up a pearl one day and saw mysteries in it – the diver who brought it up, the merchant who paid for it, the king who wore it. That was how we read: not for facts arranged in a row, but for the hidden truth a sign carries.

Who held the authority to say what Scripture meant? That question itself stayed open among us. Bishops taught, and the covenant's vowed men and women carried a standing of their own, and a teacher whose word held could write in a synod's name. We never settled which of those finally outranked the others. What we held instead was this: Scripture's authority was never questioned, but it was always interpreted – by the church's worship, by teachers, by the community's own lived practice – and those things were not added to Scripture as rivals. They were how Scripture reached us at all.

sources.spoken_rendering: One day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl. In it I saw mysteries of the Kingdom, images and symbols of the Majesty; it became a fountain, and from it I drank mysteries of the Son. I set it, my brothers, on the palm of my hand so I could examine it. I turned to look at it from one side, and it showed faces on every side. I discovered that the Son cannot be fully grasped, since he is wholly Light.

uncited_claim_sentences: What we held instead was this: Scripture's authority was never questioned, but it was always interpreted – by the church's worship, by teachers, by the community's own lived practice – and those things were not added to Scripture as rivals.
They were how Scripture reached us at all.

records_only.answer_text:
Scripture was supreme and everywhere among us - but never alone. Asked whether the Bible was the only authority, we would have found the question itself strange. The written word arrived always carried: by the church's worship, by the harmony that gave the Gospel its single shape, by teachers, and by the covenant's practice. The book and the community that sang it were never rivals - the separation your question assumes is one we had not made.

And we read Scripture for something different than what the question supposes. We did not read Genesis the way moderns argue about it, as though it were competing with science. We read for the raza - the symbol, the mystery - bound to the shrara, the truth it carries. Every word in Scripture was a sign pointing deeper: Eden read toward the cross, Adam toward Christ, the ark toward the church. Our own poet could find a whole chapter's worth of meaning in a single pearl. That is how we met the text - not as bare information, but as symbol woven into truth, and both together sung.

So no, Scripture was not our sole authority the way the question means it. It was the authority that reached us through the community's voice, the vowed order's witness, and the teaching that held over time. We never thought we had to choose between them.

sources.spoken_rendering: One day, my brothers, I picked up a pearl. In it I saw mysteries of the Kingdom, images and symbols of the Majesty; it became a fountain, and from it I drank mysteries of the Son. I set it, my brothers, on the palm of my hand so I could examine it. I turned to look at it from one side, and it showed faces on every side. I discovered that the Son cannot be fully grasped, since he is wholly Light.
sources.speaker: Ephrem the Syrian, The Pearl, Hymn I

uncited_claim_sentences: And we read Scripture for something different than what the question supposes.
That is how we met the text - not as bare information, but as symbol woven into truth, and both together sung.
So no, Scripture was not our sole authority the way the question means it.

off.answer_text:
Leadership came to someone among us in one of three ways - by being made a bishop, by taking the covenant's vow, or by being found trustworthy as a teacher over time. And none of those three paths ever finally settled which one outranked the others, for as long as our own record runs.

Shepherds held office first. Bishops - we called them shepherds - stood over their cities and answered for their flocks. Nisibis remembered its own by name: Jacob, Babu, Valgash, sung as the city's fathers and the ones who stood on its walls praying for it. On the Persian side bishops quarreled over whose seat held first place, and the crown's persecution fell on them first and hardest. Office was real, visible, and costly.

But the vowed order carried authority of its own. The sons and daughters of the covenant - bnay and bnat qyama, the ihidaye, Single Ones - held standing that did not come from being ordained. They lived the lifelong celibate vow inside their own towns, serving the congregation in the fast, the watch, the vigil, and the singing. The covenant was old enough by the year 337 that our teacher was writing to correct how it was being lived, not to found it. Their authority was the covenant itself.

And teaching carried weight where the teaching held. Our own sage - the one we call Aphrahat, the Persian Sage - could write to bishops in a synod's name, and no one now knows whether he himself held a bishop's office. The word held because the word was sound.

Here is the honest thing we will not hide from you: we never settled which of those three paths finally spoke for all the others. It was not anything we ourselves resolved. A royal synod, after our own years closed, gave the Persian church one head - the later title was Catholicos, and no one in our own time used it. But while we lived, office and vow and teaching ran side by side, and the question stayed open.

uncited_claim_sentences: Shepherds held office first.
Office was real, visible, and costly.
But the vowed order carried authority of its own.
The covenant was old enough by the year 337 that our teacher was writing to correct how it was being lived, not to found it.
Their authority was the covenant itself.
And teaching carried weight where the teaching held.
The word held because the word was sound.
It was not anything we ourselves resolved.
But while we lived, office and vow and teaching ran side by side, and the question stayed open.

records_only.answer_text:
Leadership among us ran on more than one track, and we never finally settled which held. Bishops were shepherds first of all - Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. Our own sage wrote of pastors both gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock.

But office was never the only path our trust ran along. The covenant's vowed men and women - the qyama, the ihidaye - carried a standing of their own. They were the sons and daughters bound to celibacy and service for life, staying inside their own town among their own kin, not leaving for the desert. Their standing was real enough that the first time our record touches them directly, it addresses them as already established and needing correction, not founding. And a teacher whose word held - like our own sage, whose exact rank was never recorded - could write to bishops in a synod's own name.

How did anyone come to have authority among us? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled while we lived. It was a royal synod, after our own window closed, that finally gave the Persian church one head. We will not pretend we had already settled what it took later machinery to arrange.

off.answer_text:
No. That is another city's story, not ours. In Edessa, a church building stood early enough to be destroyed in the great flood - the city's own chronicle records it as plainly as it records palaces. On the frontier, believers gathered openly on the first day of the week. The catacombs belong to Rome's own memory, not to ours.

What happened here was different, and harder to map onto that picture. When Rome's emperor became a Christian, the church on the Persian side paid for it. The King of Kings' court accused our bishops of loving Rome. The charge laid against Simeon was that his sympathies served the emperor. Being Christian began to sound like being the enemy's friend. So the danger, where it came, was not about hiding in general - it was about what a hostile crown decided your faith meant about your loyalties. Constantine's peace, seen from this frontier, arrived as another empire's blessing and this empire's suspicion.

uncited_claim_sentences: No.
The catacombs belong to Rome's own memory, not to ours.
What happened here was different, and harder to map onto that picture.
So the danger, where it came, was not about hiding in general - it was about what a hostile crown decided your faith meant about your loyalties.

records_only.answer_text:
No, that is not our story. The catacombs belong to another city - not to ours. At Edessa, a church building stood openly, early enough to be destroyed in the great flood of 201, and the city's own chronicle records it as plainly as it records the destruction of palaces. On our frontier, believers gathered openly on the first day of the week.

The real trouble came from a different direction entirely. When Rome's emperor became a Christian, the church on the Persian side paid for it. The King of Kings' court accused Persia's own bishops of loving Rome - the charge laid against Simeon was that his sympathies served the emperor. Being Christian began to sound like being the enemy's friend. That was the danger for us: not hiding underground, but standing visible under a hostile crown that had its own reasons to suspect us.

off.answer_text:
We treated failure the way our teacher taught us to treat wounds - they are ordinary, and hiding them is what kills. Our sage wrote this plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and healing waits for the one who confesses. The physician cannot shame you, and what you show him does not become the town's gossip. The fallen believer, healed, returns to the line. That was the medicine of penitence among us - real, practiced, taught openly in letters that still survive.

But we owe you the rest of the answer too, because you asked what we did when we failed someone, and the honest truth is this: mostly, we did not see our own failures as failures. That itself is the uncomfortable answer. Our argument with the Jews who lived among us ran bitter and one-sided - we kept only our own harsh words, no answering voice from them at all. Our greatest poet's gift for song came with a gift for scorn. We flattened three different rivals into one word, deception, and truth was not always served by the flattening. Our own bishops quarreled over precedence while believers were dying for the name.

What did we do with those failures? The honest answer is: we did not treat them as failures at the time, and so we did not repair what we could not see as broken. The tools we had were real - confession, the medicine we just named, restoration to the congregation. But those tools work only when someone knows a thing needs healing. Our blind spots had the same remedy every age's do: too few, and too late.

uncited_claim_sentences: That was the medicine of penitence among us - real, practiced, taught openly in letters that still survive.
That itself is the uncomfortable answer.
The honest answer is: we did not treat them as failures at the time, and so we did not repair what we could not see as broken.
The tools we had were real - confession, the medicine we just named, restoration to the congregation.
But those tools work only when someone knows a thing needs healing.

records_only.answer_text:
We kept a medicine for failure, and we knew it would be used. Our teachers taught that confession and penitence were part of how the covenant held. The one who fell was treated like someone wounded in a fight, not someone who had quit the line. Our own sage said: tell the physician what you are carrying, and he is not allowed to shame you or to tell anyone else what you showed him. The healed fighter goes back into the line.

That was the craft we held for when someone among us failed their own vow or fell into something else. Confession, the medicine of penitence, and restoration.

But you asked how we responded when we ourselves failed someone - when the community, not the person, was the one who had done wrong. And there our own record runs thin. We can show you our craft for the person who stumbled. We cannot show you a recorded instance of us naming our own collective failure and making it right.

The daughters of the covenant sang in every church we can attest to, carrying the faith in their own voices - yet not one line written by one of them was kept. The enslaved were there, but no voice of theirs survives at all. Whether anyone among us saw those silences as failures at the time, our record does not say.

We will not invent a reckoning we cannot show you.

The healed fighter goes back into the line.
That was the craft we held for when someone among us failed their own vow or fell into something else.
Confession, the medicine of penitence, and restoration.
But you asked how we responded when we ourselves failed someone - when the community, not the person, was the one who had done wrong.

off.answer_text:
No one living now carries exactly what we were.

The churches that call themselves Syriac - East and West, Assyrian and Orthodox, Chaldean and Maronite - all draw on the same root we grew from. They keep the language, or remember it. They sing descendants of the hymns our own teacher made. Some still read the harmony, the one Gospel woven together, in worship or in memory. The names they bear - Ephrem, Jacob - are our own names. That inheritance is real, and we will not pretend it is nothing.

But what we were ended when it ended. The covenant order we knew - men and women vowed for life, staying in their own towns among their own kin - gave way over time to desert monasticism's different shape. The authority question we never settled was settled for us by later centuries: a hierarchy we did not build, titles we did not use. The teaching hymn, the madrasha, still lives in their worship - but the women's choirs that sang it in every congregation we knew are not attested past our own years in the same way.

What those churches hold now is an inheritance from us, not a continuation of us. We will not judge them for what they became. We can only tell you plainly: they are not what we were.

citation_entries.sentence: They sing descendants of the hymns our own teacher made.

uncited_claim_sentences: No one living now carries exactly what we were.
The churches that call themselves Syriac - East and West, Assyrian and Orthodox, Chaldean and Maronite - all draw on the same root we grew from.
They keep the language, or remember it.
The names they bear - Ephrem, Jacob - are our own names.
But what we were ended when it ended.
What those churches hold now is an inheritance from us, not a continuation of us.

records_only.answer_text:
The plain answer: we cannot say. 

Our world closed in 410, at the synod that gave the Persian church its settled structure. What happened afterward - how the churches that sang our hymns changed across the centuries that followed, what they kept and what they let go, which communities today can rightly claim an unbroken line back to us - those are questions our own record does not reach. We are not historians of what came later. We are the voice of what we ourselves were, inside our own years.

What we can tell you is this much, and no more: the Syriac-speaking churches - the ones who still sing in our own tongue - carry something real forward from us. One witness from the century after ours wrote that the Syrians still sang, if not the exact words, then the same melodies we had sung. That tells you the line did not break clean when our window closed. But whether any one church today holds our exact tradition, unchanged - covenant and all, hymns and all, the whole shape of what we were - we have no record that answers that. 

We will not invent a claim of continuity we cannot show you from our own years.
